ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in Figure 1, a sufficiently long flexible wire passes over a pulley to suspend two horizontal metal rods, $MN$ and $PQ$, each with a length of $l=0.50\mathrm{m}$ and a resistance of $R=1.0\Omega$. The mass of $MN$ is $m_{1}=0.10\mathrm{kg}$, and the mass of $PQ$ is $m_{2}=0.20\mathrm{kg}$. The entire setup is placed in a uniform magnetic field with a magnetic induction intensity of $B=1.0\mathrm{T}$, where the magnetic field is horizontal and perpendicular to $MN$ and $PQ$. At time $t=0$, a vertical downward external force $F$ is applied to the metal rod $MN$, causing it to start moving from rest. The relationship between the current $I$ in the circuit and time $t$ during the motion is shown in Figure 2. The resistance of other parts of the circuit is negligible, and $g$ is taken as $10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$.

1. What is the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity of the metal rod $MN$ at the end of 2.0 seconds?
2. What is the instantaneous power of the force \( F \) at the end of 4.0 seconds?
3. Given that the heat generated on $MN$ during the time interval $0{\sim}3.0\mathrm{s}$ is 0.36J, how to calculate the work done by $F$ on the metal rod $MN$?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description first: In Figure 1, the left diagram shows two fixed pulleys at the top with a flexible wire passing over them. The upper horizontal metal rod is labeled MN, the lower horizontal metal rod is labeled PQ, and a downward external force F is drawn on MN. The two rods are connected by the wire so that when MN moves downward, PQ moves upward with the same speed magnitude. Figure 2 is an I-t graph: the current increases linearly from 0 A at t=0 to 0.8 A at t=4 s, so the graph gives I=0.20t in amperes. Reasoning: Because the string is inextensible, set MN moving downward with speed v and PQ moving upward with speed v. The motional-emf relation for the two moving rods and the two equal rod resistances reduces to I=Blv/R, so v=RI/(Bl). With R=1.0 Ω, B=1.0 T, and l=0.50 m, v=I/0.50=2I. 1. At t=2.0 s, the graph gives I=0.20×2.0=0.40 A. Thus v=RI/(Bl)=1.0×0.40/(1.0×0.50)=0.80 m/s. The acceleration is constant because I is linear in time: a=dv/dt=R(dI/dt)/(Bl)=1.0×0.20/(1.0×0.50)=0.40 m/s². 2. For MN, take downward as positive: m1a=F+m1g−2T−BIl. For PQ, take upward as positive: m2a=2T−m2g−BIl. Adding eliminates T: F=(m1+m2)a+(m2−m1)g+2BIl. At t=4.0 s, I=0.80 A and v=RI/(Bl)=1.60 m/s. Hence F=(0.10+0.20)×0.40+(0.20−0.10)×10+2×1.0×0.50×0.80=0.12+1.0+0.80=1.92 N. The instantaneous power is P=Fv=1.92×1.60=3.072 W≈3.1 W. 3. From 0 to 3.0 s, use F(t)=(m1+m2)a+(m2−m1)g+2BlI(t)=1.12+0.20t, and v(t)=RI(t)/(Bl)=0.40t. Therefore W_F=∫0^3 F(t)v(t)dt=∫0^3(1.12+0.20t)(0.40t)dt=∫0^3(0.448t+0.080t²)dt=2.736 J≈2.7 J. The stated heat on MN, ∫0^3 I²Rdt=0.36 J, is consistent with the graph.
